vt5_recognition.topic: Holy See as subject of international law; diplomatic relations; UN observer status; See Change campaign

claims.text: Holy See Press Office note of 9 January 2026: 184 states have diplomatic relations with the Holy See, plus the European Union and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta; 93 embassy chancelleries accredited to the Holy See are based in Rome; offices of the League of Arab States, IOM and UNHCR accredited to the Holy See are in Rome. The note lists no new relations in 2025.

Between 1870 and 1929, with no territory, the Holy See continued to send and receive diplomats; states with relations rose from 16 to 27; it concluded 29 concordats and agreements and was asked to mediate 13 international disputes; some jurists doubted its standing.

The 184 include 181 UN member states, Palestine, the Republic of China (Taiwan) and the Cook Islands; the Holy See lacks relations with 12 UN members, including the People's Republic of China, Saudi Arabia, Vietnam, Afghanistan, North Korea; UK relations 16 January 1982; US relations 10 January 1984; latest: Palestine 13 May 2015, Myanmar 4 May 2017, Oman 23 February 2023.

The Holy See became a Permanent Observer State at the UN on 6 April 1964. UNGA resolution 58/314, adopted 1 July 2004 at the 92nd plenary meeting, granted rights including participation in the general debate, the right of reply, raising points of order on matters concerning it (without challenging the chair) and co-sponsoring draft resolutions referring to it; it 'shall not have the right to vote or to put forward candidates'.
The resolution was adopted by consensus on 1 July 2004, as the mission marked the fortieth anniversary of its presence (Migliore statement).

On 14 March 2000 Frances Kissling (Catholics for a Free Choice) and others presented the See Change campaign at UN Headquarters, asking Kofi Annan to review the Holy See's non-member state permanent observer status and to give it NGO status like the World Council of Churches; almost 400 organizations had endorsed; Anika Rahman argued it met only one of the four criteria of statehood.

RNS: Kissling claimed 500 endorsing organizations; the US bishops called CFFC's teaching undeserving of recognition; former US ambassador Ray Flynn and others defended the Holy See's role; counter-campaigns formed.
The Holy See–China Provisional Agreement on the appointment of bishops, signed 22 September 2018, renewed for two years in 2020 and 2022, was extended for four years on 22 October 2024.

vt5_immunity.topic: Sovereign immunity of the Holy See in national and European courts

claims.text: Doe v. Holy See (D. Or.): suit over abuse c. 1965 by Fr Andrew Ronan; Ninth Circuit, 3 March 2009 (557 F.3d 1066), allowed the case to proceed against the Holy See under the FSIA on Oregon's definition of employment.
The US Supreme Court declined review on 28 June 2010; Holy See counsel Jeffrey Lena said the decision 'is not a comment on the merits'.
On 20 August 2012 Judge Michael Mosman held the facts did not establish an employer-employee relationship between Ronan and the Holy See, and dismissed the claim.

O'Bryan v. Holy See: Sixth Circuit, 24 November 2008, held the Holy See is a foreign state under the FSIA; claims on the conduct of bishops and Holy See personnel supervising clergy in the US could proceed under the tortious-act exception; claims based on the abuse itself and on Holy See acts abroad could not.

In August 2010 plaintiffs' attorney William McMurry dropped O'Bryan, citing the high bar of sovereign immunity and the lack of further plaintiffs; Lena (9 August) said it confirmed 'there has never been a Holy See policy requiring concealment of child sexual abuse'.

J.C. and Others v. Belgium (ECtHR, 12 October 2021): 24 applicants alleging abuse by priests; Belgian courts (Ghent first instance 2013, appeal February 2016) upheld the Holy See's immunity; the Court found no violation of Article 6 §1, treating it as reasonable to regard the Holy See as having the characteristics of a foreign state; the bishops' conduct was not attributable to the Holy See and the Holy See's alleged failures occurred in Rome.

vt5_treaty_bodies.topic: UN treaty bodies: CRC and CAT reviews of the Holy See, 2014, and the Holy See's replies

claims.text: The Holy See ratified the CRC on 20 April 1990 and the CAT on 26 June 2002; it is party to CERD (1969), the Geneva Conventions and the 1951 Refugee Convention; it has not signed the ICCPR, ICESCR or CEDAW.

CRC concluding observations (CRC/C/VAT/CO/2, 25 Feb 2014): ratification committed the Holy See to implement the Convention 'not only within the territory of Vatican City State, but also, as the supreme power of the Catholic Church, worldwide'; known abusers were 'transferred from parish to parish or to other countries'; reporting to police 'has never been made compulsory'; a 'code of silence' on clergy under penalty of excommunication; recommended removing abusers, referring them to law enforcement, mandatory reporting, opening archives; also on corporal punishment, Magdalene laundries, abortion (canon 1398), contraception, gender stereotyping; noted the Commission for the Protection of Minors announced 5 December 2013; reservations condition application on compatibility with Vatican City State law.

Tomasi to the CRC, 16 January 2014: distinguished the Holy See, Vatican City State and local Churches; abuse cases 'have rightly been adjudicated and punished by the competent civil authorities in the respective countries'; VCS Laws VIII and IX of 11 July 2013 gave penal jurisdiction over crimes abroad by its public officials.

Holy See statement, 5 February 2014: 'takes note' of the observations, which 'will be submitted to a thorough study and examination'; it objected to 'an attempt to interfere with Catholic Church teaching'; Tomasi said the document seemed 'prepared before' the January hearing.

CAT concluding observations (CAT/C/VAT/CO/1, 17 June 2014): delegation reported 3,420 credible allegations confirmed by the CDF 2004-2013, 848 priests defrocked, 2,572 otherwise disciplined; Committee found the interpretative declaration limiting the Convention not consistent and said obligations apply to officials 'wherever they exercise effective control over persons or territory'; concern that officials 'resist the principle of mandatory reporting'; asked about Archbishop Wesolowski; follow-up due 23 May 2015.

Holy See communiqué 23 May 2014: observations 'include many positive outcomes'; rejected the 'implicit fundamental assumption' equating sexual abuse with torture as 'fundamentally flawed'; the CAT 'applies to Vatican City State'; priests worldwide are not 'indirectly legally dependent' on the Vatican; the committee's role is 'to monitor and report, and not to adjudicate'.

Kieran Tapsell (Dec 2025): Holy See reported to the CRC in 1994 and 2011 and had filed no report since; after 2014 it said its obligation ran only to children in Vatican City; he urged Leo XIV to submit a report.

vt5_moneyval_euro.topic: EU Monetary Agreement 2009, AIF/ASIF and MONEYVAL evaluations

claims.text: The Monetary Agreement between the EU (Commission and Italy) and Vatican City State (represented by the Holy See) was signed at Brussels on 17 December 2009 by Joaquín Almunia and Archbishop André Dupuy, entered into force 1 January 2010 and repealed the agreement of 29 December 2000; Art. 1 euro legal tender; Art. 2 no own banknotes or coins without EU agreement; Art. 3 coin ceiling (fixed part EUR 2.3m for 2010 plus variable part); Art. 8 obliges Vatican City to implement listed EU acts on euro notes and coins, preventing money laundering, fraud and counterfeiting, medals and tokens, and statistics.

Commission Decision (EU) 2025/898 of 15 May 2025 updated the Annex (amended yearly under Art. 8(3)), with deadlines e.g. 31 December 2026 for Regulation 2023/1113 and 31 December 2028 for Regulations 2024/1624 and 2024/1620 and Directive 2024/1640; deadlines agreed by the Joint Committee 2013-2024; annex includes a section on entities carrying out financial activities on a professional basis.

Benedict XVI established the Financial Information Authority (AIF) by motu proprio of 30 December 2010; Francis strengthened it by motu proprio 8 August 2013 and Law XVIII of 8 October 2013 and gave it new statutes 15 November 2013; functions: prudential supervision, AML/CFT, financial intelligence.

AIF gained prudential supervision in August 2013; on 5 December 2020 new statutes renamed it the Supervisory and Financial Information Authority (ASIF); Carmelo Barbagallo president from 27 November 2019.

MONEYVAL 2012 report (MONEYVAL(2012)17, 4 July 2012, 39th plenary): of 16 core and key recommendations, 9 rated compliant or largely compliant and 7 partially or non-compliant; the AIF's independence and powers were unclear and 'no inspections have been undertaken'; it 'strongly recommended that IOR is also supervised by a prudential supervisor'; the law was 'wholly supplanted and replaced' by Decree CLIX of 25 January 2012.

The Holy See applied to MONEYVAL in 2011; progress reports 2013, 2015, 2017; IOR remediation led to closure of about 4,800 accounts; by late 2017 AIF had made 69 disseminations to the Promoter of Justice since 2013, no case had reached court or confiscation.

The Egmont Group suspended the AIF on 13 November 2019 after the Vatican Gendarmerie's 1 October 2019 raid on the Secretariat of State and AIF; revoked 22 January 2020 after a memorandum with the Promoter of Justice.

MONEYVAL 2021 (MONEYVAL(2021)4, adopted at the 61st plenary 26-30 April 2021, on-site visit 30 September-13 October 2020): effectiveness 5 substantial, 6 moderate, none low; R.13 (correspondent banking) non-compliant; concerns: insider risk, under-resourced prosecution, protracted investigations, minimal sanctions, gap between seized and confiscated; two self-laundering convictions 2018 and 2019, a third 21 January 2021; confiscations about EUR 1.3m.
Holy See Press Office, 9 June 2021: 'welcomes the Moneyval Report' and 'renews its commitment to continue working towards full compliance'.

MONEYVAL follow-up adopted at its 67th plenary, 20-24 May 2024: R.13 upgraded from non-compliant to compliant; R.16 and R.24 from partially to largely compliant; next technical-compliance assessment in about four years (sixth round); the Holy See is a MONEYVAL member.
ASIF 2024 annual report: 79 suspicious activity reports (123 in 2023); 11 reports to the Promoter of Justice.
